extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy; rulers, statesmen, and students of moral-political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the duties and practical standards for sovereign government (application of punishments and rewards, selection of counsellors and commanders) and of the nature, promulgation, and proper forms of divine law and worship as derived from natural reason and revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of Punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: The end of punishing is not revenge but correction (of the offender or of others by his example); the severest punishments should be inflicted for crimes most dangerous to the public (those proceeding from malice to the government, contempt of justice, provoking public indignation, or which if unpunished seem authorised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lenity is appropriate for crimes of infirmity (provocation, fear, need, ignorance) when it does not prejudice the commonwealth; punish leaders/teachers of a commotion rather than the poor seduced people; be mindful punishment of ignorance may reflect sovereign's failure to instruct. Example: Tarquin—one son's insolence provoked expulsion and dissolution of monarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle for Applying Rewards
rubrics_metrics.description: Rewards belong to the sovereign and must be applied so as to benefit the commonwealth; their use and end is to recompense past service in a way that encourages others to serve and to improve their ability to serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewards should be given with as little expense to the public purse as possible while still encouraging service; avoiding buying off ambitious popular subjects (which is not reward but bribery) because it breeds more ambition and public harm (Hydra metaphor). It is better to oppose beginnings of aspirants to greatness with small dangers than to reward and later face greater ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of Counsellors
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign must choose good counsellors — those most able and whose advice he will take in government; this choice is peculiar to monarchy because in other forms counsellors are members of the sovereign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer counsellors who have least hope of benefit from giving evil counsel and who know most about matters that conduce to peace and defence; watch signs of self-interested advisers (soothing people over grievances when their estates are insufficient). Good signs of knowledge: much conversing in the art and constant good effects. Counsell does not come by lot or inheritance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and Method of Counselling
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsell is more beneficial when each counsellor gives his advice and reasons apart, and when advice is premeditated rather than sudden or delivered as orations in assembly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premeditation allows survey of consequences and reduces error from envy, emulation, or other passions; individual, reasoned advice is preferred over public oratorical assemblies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sourcing Domestic Policy Advice from Provinces
rubrics_metrics.description: For laws concerned only with the inward ease and benefit of subjects, the best counsel is to be taken from general informations and complaints of the people of each province, who are best acquainted with their own wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such local knowledge should be diligently taken notice of so long as requests do not derogate from essential rights of sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities Required of a Commander in Chief
rubrics_metrics.description: A commander must be industrious, valiant, affable, liberal, and fortunate so as to gain opinion of sufficiency and love of his soldiers; popularity in the commander breeds desire and courage in soldiers to recommend themselves to his favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Popularity allows the general to punish mutinous or negligent soldiers effectively, but care is required because the soldiers' affection can endanger sovereign power if the commander’s fidelity is doubtful; the sovereign should ensure both good conductors and faithful subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Sovereign Popularity on Military Danger
rubrics_metrics.description: When the sovereign himself is popular (reverenced and beloved), the popularity of subordinate subjects (e.g., commanders) poses no danger to sovereign power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A known right to sovereign power makes a ruler's title sufficiently popular so he need not rely on other means to turn subjects' hearts; usurpers must fabricate titles to avoid public shame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign Rights in Inter-State (Law of Nations) Context
rubrics_metrics.description: The law commonly called the Law of Nations is the same as the Law of Nature; sovereigns have the same right in procuring the safety of their people that individuals have in procuring their own safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every sovereign may exercise rights to secure his people analogous to natural individual rights; there is no external court of natural justice beyond conscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who Are Subjects in the Kingdom of God (Criterion of Subjecthood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects in the kingdom of God are those who believe God governs the world, has given precepts, and propounded rewards and punishments to mankind; atheists and those who deny God's providence are not subjects but to be understood as enemies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belief in divine governance, hope of rewards, and fear of punishments are required for subjecthood; mere denial of God's providence removes the relation of subject to sovereign God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promulgation Requirement for Law (Divine and Civil)
rubrics_metrics.description: To be law, words must be manifestly made known with sufficient and clear promulgation such as may take away the excuse of ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: God declares his laws three ways (natural reason, revelation, and voice of a person accredited by miracles), corresponding to different modes of human hearing (right reason, sense supernatural, faith). Without promulgation a rule cannot be treated as binding law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple and Twofold Word of God (Modes of Divine Legislation)
rubrics_metrics.description: God's word arises threefold — rational (dictates of natural reason), sensible (revelation), and prophetical (voice of a person accredited by miracles) — and therefore there is a twofold kingdom of God: natural (governed by reason) and prophetical (positive laws given to a chosen nation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different modes require different epistemic attitudes (reason, supernatural sense, faith); universal laws by revelation/inspiration have not been given in the same universal manner as natural reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of God's Sovereignty (Basis of Right to Punish)
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of God to reign and to afflict men is derived from his irresistible power (omnipotence), not merely from being creator or gracious; dominion adheres to those whose power is irresistible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment may be due for sin, but the right of afflicting is also grounded in power; this explains why the prosperity/adversity distribution is justified by divine power rather than human accounts of sin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divine Laws: Moral Duties vs Honor of God
rubrics_metrics.description: Divine laws, as dictated by natural reason, concern either natural duties of one man to another (equity, justice, mercy, humility, etc.) or the honour and worship due to the Divine Majesty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The moral virtues previously discussed (chaps 14–15) are the first set; the chapter focuses on what natural reason dictates concerning honour and worship of God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and Ends of Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: Honour is an inward opinion of another's power and goodness; worship (cultus) are external signs (words and actions) expressive of that opinion; the end of worship among men is power (to make another's power greater by prompting obedience), while worship of God proceeds from duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate culture (labour to benefit subject to us) from cultus (winning favour from those not subject to us); worship should reflect the highest possible opinion of God's power and goodness and not be directed toward selfish ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions in Worship: Natural vs Arbitrary; Commanded vs Free; Public vs Private
rubrics_metrics.description: Some signs of honour/attributes/actions are naturally so (e.g., prayers, thanks, obedience) while others are arbitrary (gestures vary by custom); arbitrary worship itself may be commanded by the worshipped or voluntary; public worship (commonwealth) should be uniform while private worship can be free but subject to restraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public worship must be exhibited by private men in a uniform manner to count as the commonwealth's worship; where many sorts of worship are allowed there is no public worship; arbitrary signs that are shameful cannot be enjoined as divine worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes Properly Ascribed to God in Natural Worship
rubrics_metrics.description: By natural reason we ought to attribute existence, infinitude, eternity, incomprehensibility, and superlatives (Most High, Most Great), or indefinite attributes (Good, Just, Holy, Creator) to God — but avoid ascribing finite attributes, parts, place, motion, passions, or plurality of gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attributes should be stated negatively, superlatively, or indefinitely rather than in terms that circumscribe or anthropomorphize God; any attribute implying finitude, passivity, or compositeness is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions That Constitute Significant Divine Honour (List)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason prescribes certain actions as signs of intention to honour God: prayers, thanksgiving, gifts/sacrifices (of the best), not swearing by any but God, speaking considerately of God, using fitting words and gestures, public worship, and obedience to God's laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prayers/thanks should be expressed in beautifull and well-composed language (not sudden, light, or plebeian); offerings should be of the best and full of submission and remembrance of benefits; the name of God should not be used rashly except as oath ordered by the commonwealth; disputing God's nature from natural reason is dishonourable; obedience to God's laws (natural law) is the greatest worship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public Worship Requires Uniformity and Civil Enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the commonwealth is one person it ought to exhibit one public worship; public worship exists when the commonwealth commands private men to exhibit uniform signs of honour to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where multiple forms of worship are allowed (from differing private religions), there is no public worship and thus no religion of the commonwealth; attributes and signs of honour used in public worship are defined by civil law enacted by the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural Punishments as Consequences of Actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every human action begins a chain of consequences; natural punishments are the natural, not arbitrary, consequences of breaching the laws of nature (e.g., intemperance → disease; rashness → mishap; injustice → violence of enemies; pride → ruin; negligent princes → rebellion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These punishments follow as natural effects; human providence cannot always foresee the end of the chain, so natural punishments serve as corrective consequences tied to the nature of actions.
